text: The Bank of China Building on Battery Road
In May 1937, the Bank of China paid $715,000 for one of the most valuable properties in Singapore — a marble-fronted banking palace on Battery Road — and then, for ten years, did not move in.
The palace it bought, and never used, is the forgotten half of the story.
The palace had been built for another bank entirely.
The Chartered Bank's bullion palace had become a shop.

The bank's Singapore branch closed as Japanese forces overran Southeast Asia in 1942 — only its London, New York, Calcutta and Bombay offices stayed open — while back on Battery Road, remarkably, both department stores traded on through the Occupation; by July 1943 a Japanese restaurant, the Mutsumi, had opened in the building.
What followed was reported in the newspapers as Singapore's "squat" drama.
Demolition of the palazzo was under way by May, under a Malaya Tribune headline that already looked past it: "Work Begins on S'pore Skyscraper".
With the foundations complete, the branch sought — and, in May 1950, obtained — its head office's approval to build the superstructure.
The block was finished in December 1953, and on the 28th of December the Singapore Standard announced: "Bank Of China Moves Into New Building Today."
And at the Battery Road entrance stood the detail that has outlasted every argument about the building: a pair of Chinese lions in pre-cast stone, sculpted by the Italian artist Rodolfo Nolli.
But it was never the tallest building in Singapore.
What the Bank of China Building genuinely was — the tallest building on the Singapore River waterfront, and for a generation the landmark of Raffles Place — is distinction enough.

Singapore, a separate jurisdiction, was unaffected — until December 1964, in the middle of a revenue dispute between Singapore and the federal government in Kuala Lumpur, when Malaysia's finance minister announced that the Bank of China in Singapore would be closed.
The closure was never carried out.
The building today is two buildings.

For all that, the 1953 block holds no conservation status — unlike the Asia Insurance Building, gazetted in 2007 as Singapore's first protected skyscraper, the Bank of China Building stands in the middle of the financial district unlisted and largely unremarked, a first-generation skyscraper hiding in plain sight.
